blocks.text: And Artemidorus, Onirocritica, book 1, ch. 30: Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομένας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· [Pareias ischnas echein, ē helkomenas, lypas, ē penthos sēmainei. ischnas men lypas, helkomenas de penthos. kai gar en tois penthesi lōbōntai tas pareias hoi anthrōpoi] To have (in dreams) thin or ulcerated cheeks signifies sadness and mourning: thin cheeks sadness, ulcerated ones mourning. For in mourning people tear their cheeks. I admit that I have read in Horapollo, Hieroglyph. book 2, ch. 50, that the turtledove has teeth. To signify a nursing woman, and one who nourishes well, he says, they (the Egyptians) τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει [trygona zōgraphousin; hautē gar monē tōn allōn ptēnōn odontas, kai masthous echei], paint a turtledove: for this alone among birds has teeth and breasts. If this were true, it would also have jaws and cheeks. But learned men have already observed that these things belong to the bat, to which alone they apply. Some therefore change τρυγόνα [trygona] into τριγόνα [trigona], conjecturing that the bat is called by this name there, because τρίζειν [trizein, to squeak] is proper to it. Others, better, change it into νυκτερίδα [nykterida]; and why the two were interchanged, the reason is obvious. Immediately before came: Wishing to signify a weak man who attempts great things, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν [nykterida zōgraphousin], they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And immediately after follows: Intending to designate a man who is charmed by dancing and the pipe, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν [trygona zōgraphousin], they paint a turtledove, which is caught by the pipe and by dancing. I have rendered turtledove with Mercerus, Caussinus and others. Yet—and I am surprised that this escaped them—τρυγὼν [trygōn] there is not the turtledove but the stingray, which this same writer below, in ch. 105, calls simply τρυγόνα [trygona], and others, to distinguish it, θαλαττίαν τρυγόνα [thalattian trygona], sea turtledove, διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs]. For it is not the turtledove, the bird, but ἡ θαλαττία τρυγὼν [hē thalattia trygōn], the sea turtledove, that is, the stingray, that, charmed by the pipe and dancing, is led into the fish-trap, as Aelian relates at length, On Animals book 17, ch. 18—although Philo too refers this to the turtledove, the bird. Now, to return to where the discussion digressed, the words of the Sacred Song run thus in Hebrew: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Your cheeks are adorned with rows (of gems), your neck with chains. [II, 600] For which the Greeks have Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos, trachēlos sou hōs hormiskoi?] and Jerome, How beautiful your cheeks have become, like a turtledove's, your neck like a necklace. For, ב and כ being interchanged, they read כתורים for בחורים and כחרוזים for בחרוזים, and took תורי for turtledoves, whereas there it signifies rows, namely of gems or of golden studs. Many things show that it must be so rendered. 1. תורים and חרוזים are here nearly synonymous. Moreover, although the word חרוזים does not occur elsewhere in Scripture, it is very well known from the Arabic language, in which خرز [kharaza] is a verb meaning to sew with an awl, and الخرز [al-kharaz] a necklace of gems strung together, and also the spine, whose vertebrae are as it were sewn and strung together. Accordingly the Greek explains חרוזים as ὁρμισκοὺς [hormiskous], and Jerome as necklaces, quite rightly. 2. Immediately follows תורי זהב נעשה לך, where it is plain that תורי are not turtledoves but a kind of golden ornament, namely chains or something similar. Accordingly Jerome there has We will make you golden little chains [muraenulas]. And the Syriac ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ, a golden chain. And the fifth edition στρεπτὸν χρυσίου [strepton chrysiou]—so it must be read, not στρεπτοῦ [streptou]. For στρεπτὸς [streptos] or στρεπτὸν [strepton] is commonly used for a torque by Herodotus, Xenophon, Plutarch and others. In Symmachus, for περίβλεπτα χρυσίου [periblepta chrysiou] I would read περίπλεκτα [peripletka]. For στρέφειν [strephein], whence στρεπτὸν [strepton], and πλέκειν [plekein], whence πλεκτὸν [plekton], are nearly synonymous. Accordingly in Hesychius πλόκιον [plokion] is εἶδος περιδεραίου [eidos periderαiou], a kind of necklace. And the same reasoning holds for the Syriac ܥܢܩܐ for chain, for the verb ܥܢܩ means to fold and to twist. But why do the Elders render ὁμοιώματα [homoiōmata]? Did they read ציורי, that is, images, for תורי? Or did they think that תורי זהב meant likenesses of turtledoves made of gold, which was the opinion of Aben Ezra? 3. Indeed תור with Thau is here the same as טור with Teth, a word that Moses commonly uses for a row of gems: as in Exod. XXVIII, 17, ארבעה טורים אבן, four rows of stones. Likewise, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, sardius, topaz and emerald, the first row. 5. Nor is it obscure how cheeks may be adorned with rows of gems: namely, if they hang from the ears, or if they are sprinkled over the bands of the mitres, that is, broad ribbons which were drawn down along the jaws and tied under the chin. For in Syria the mitre was a woman's head-covering. Virgil in the Catalecta: [col. 58]
The Syrian hostess, her head bound with a Greek little mitre.
Go, you who fancy a barbarian harlot with a painted mitre.
Barbarian, that is, Syrian; for there had preceded:
